National Register of Historic Places listings in Baltimore
National Register of Historic Places listings in Central Baltimore

stops.name: USS Constellation
stops.description: Tied up at Pier 1 is the last sail-only warship the U.S. Navy ever built, launched in 1854 and the only intact vessel left that served in the Civil War.

stops.name: National Aquarium
stops.description: The glass-pyramid aquarium that opened on Pier 3 in 1981 anchored the rebuilt Inner Harbor and is now the most visited attraction in Maryland.

stops.name: Reginald F. Lewis Museum of Maryland African American History and Culture
stops.description: Opened in 2005 and named for the first Black American to build a billion-dollar company, this Smithsonian affiliate holds some 11,000 objects covering four centuries of Black Maryland.

stops.name: Star-Spangled Banner Flag House
stops.description: Mary Pickersgill stitched the enormous 15-star garrison flag that flew over Fort McHenry in this 1793 brick house, which is why the anthem exists.

stops.name: Carroll Mansion
stops.description: Charles Carroll of Carrollton, the last surviving signer of the Declaration of Independence, spent his final twelve winters in this 1811 Federal townhouse and died here.

stops.name: Lloyd Street Synagogue
stops.description: Maryland's first synagogue, finished in 1845 in Greek Revival stone, hides the oldest known mikveh in the country beneath its floor.

stops.name: Phoenix Shot Tower
stops.description: Molten lead was dropped 215 feet down the middle of this 1828 brick cylinder to make musket shot, and for eighteen years it was the tallest structure in America.

stops.name: The Peale
stops.description: Rembrandt Peale put up this 1814 building as the first structure in the Western Hemisphere purpose-built to be a museum, and it reopened as one in 2022 after a long detour as City Hall and a Black grammar school.

stops.name: Baltimore City Hall
stops.description: A 22-year-old architect won the commission for this white marble Second Empire pile with its cast-iron dome, finished in 1875 and still the mayor's address.

stops.name: War Memorial Building
stops.description: Dedicated in 1925 across the plaza from City Hall, its marble auditorium walls carry the names of 1,752 Marylanders killed in the First World War.

stops.name: Battle Monument
stops.description: Begun in 1815 for the defenders who died holding Baltimore against the British, this was the first war memorial in the country to list the dead of every rank together.

stops.name: Basilica of the National Shrine of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary
stops.description: Benjamin Latrobe designed the first Catholic cathedral built in the United States, opened in 1821 in deliberately plain neoclassical lines rather than Gothic ones.

stops.name: Emerson Bromo-Seltzer Tower
stops.description: The four 24-foot clock faces on this 1911 tower spell BROMO SELTZER where the numbers should be, and a 51-foot glowing blue medicine bottle rotated on top until 1936.

stops.name: Old Otterbein United Methodist Church
stops.description: Built in 1785 by German Reformed families and still holding services, this is the oldest church building in Baltimore, with bells cast in Germany and hung in 1789.

stops.name: Baltimore and Ohio Warehouse at Camden Yards
stops.description: The 1,116-foot railroad warehouse the Orioles built their ballpark against in 1992 has never been hit by a fair ball in a regulation game.

note: First Baltimore run. 15 stops, all verified against their own Wikipedia articles, forming a loop from the Inner Harbor east into Jonestown, north to the City Hall / War Memorial civic core, then west past the Basilica and Bromo tower and back down to Camden Yards. All still standing, all publicly accessible or visible from the street. ZIP filled on 14 of 15. Battle Monument has no street number - it stands in the median of N Calvert St between E Fayette and E Lexington - so address and zip are left null rather than invented; a human can pin it from the article coordinates. Dropped deliberately: Lexington Market (real and open, but 1.1 mi northwest of the harbor and its historic shed was replaced by new construction in 2022 - worth a later run if the cluster is widened), Statue of Christopher Columbus (removed from its plinth in 2020), Ford's Grand Opera House and Eutaw House (both demolished), and the several dozen geotagged downtown office towers and transit stations that carry articles but are not places anyone would stop and look at.
